title: Triangulation from the abstract dg-category axioms A, B and C
statement:
Let $\mathcal A$ be a small cochain dg category over $\mathbf Z$ (a set of objects, cochain complexes of abelian groups $\mathcal A(x,y)$ as morphism objects, and associative unital compositions $\mathcal A(y,z)\otimes\mathcal A(x,y)\to\mathcal A(x,z)$ which are chain maps, so that $\partial(gh)=(\partial g)h+(-1)^{|g|}g\partial h$ for homogeneous $g,h$). Write $Z^0\mathcal A$ for its category of closed degree-zero maps and $H^0\mathcal A$ for its category of degree-zero cohomology classes. Assume (A) there is a zero object and each pair $x,z$ has a dg direct sum: an object with closed degree-zero inclusions and projections satisfying the biproduct identities. Assume (B) there are dg functors $[n]$, $n\in\mathbf Z$, with $[0]=1$, $[n+m]=[n][m]$, and isomorphisms of cochain complexes $\mathcal A(x,y[n])\cong\mathcal A(x,y)[n]$ compatible with composition, with $V[n]^j=V^{j+n}$ and $d_{V[n]}=(-1)^nd_V$.

Call a sequence $x\xrightarrow{a}y\xrightarrow{b}z$ in $Z^0\mathcal A$ admissible if there are degree-zero graded maps $\pi:y\to x$ and $s:z\to y$ with $\pi a=1$, $bs=1$, $a\pi+sb=1$, $ba=0$, and $\pi s=0$. For such a splitting, the degree-one closed map $\pi\partial s$ corresponds under (B) to a closed degree-zero map $\delta:z\to x[1]$. Assume (C) that for every $f:x\to y$ in $Z^0\mathcal A$ there is an admissible sequence $y\xrightarrow{i}c(f)\xrightarrow{p}x[1]$ whose associated boundary $x[1]\to y[1]$ is $f[1]$.

Then $H^0\mathcal A$, with the induced translations and triangles isomorphic to the admissible-sequence triangles $(x,y,z,a,b,\delta)$, is a triangulated category in the sense of [def-weil-triangulated-category]. These distinguished triangles are precisely those isomorphic to $(x,y,c(f),f,i,-p)$ for closed degree-zero $f$, with cones as in (C).

proof.text: The Leibniz identity makes boundaries an ideal among closed degree-zero maps: if $\partial a=\partial b=0$ and $h$ has degree $-1$, then $b\partial h=\partial(bh)$ and $(\partial h)a=\partial(ha)$. Thus composition descends to the abelian-group quotients $H^0\mathcal A(x,y)$. The closed inclusions and projections in (A) retain their biproduct equations in this quotient, so it is additive with zero object. The dg functors in (B) act additively on these quotients and have strict inverses $[-n]$.

source.place: Section-review, axioms (A),(B), and Tag 09QW: additive structure before TR1.

proof.text: For an admissible sequence $(a,b,\pi,s)$, differentiating $bs=1$, $\pi a=1$, and $a\pi+sb=1$ gives $b\partial s=0$, $(\partial\pi)a=0$, and $a\partial\pi+(\partial s)b=0$. Multiplying by $a\pi+sb$ gives $\partial s=a\pi\partial s$ and $\partial\pi=(\partial\pi)sb$. Differentiating $\pi s=0$ gives $\delta=\pi\partial s=-(\partial\pi)s$. Hence $a\delta=\partial s$, $\delta b=-\partial\pi$; also $a\partial\delta=\partial(a\delta)=0$, whence $\partial\delta=\pi a\partial\delta=0$. These are precisely the closed boundary and the null composite classes required for the associated triangle, with the shift identifications of (B).

The class of the boundary does not depend on the graded splitting. For another splitting $(\pi\prime,s\prime)$ of the same closed sequence, $s\prime-s=a\pi s\prime$ and $\pi\prime a=1$. Since $\partial s=a\delta$, we have $\pi\prime\partial s=\delta$. Consequently $\delta\prime=\pi\prime\partial(s+a\pi s\prime)=\delta+\pi\prime a\partial(\pi s\prime)=\delta+\partial(\pi s\prime)$. Under (B), the last term is a boundary in the complex defining the arrow $z\to x[1]$, so both splittings define the same arrow in $H^0\mathcal A$.

For an admissible sequence $x\xrightarrow{a}y\xrightarrow{b}z$, part (i) of the cone-comparison lemma gives an isomorphism, with identities on $x,y$, from $(x,y,c(a),a,i_a,-p_a)$ to its associated triangle. Conversely, for a closed $f:x\to y$, apply admissible replacement with $N=2$ to obtain $x\xrightarrow{j}\widetilde y$ admissible and a homotopy equivalence $r:\widetilde y\to y$ with $rj=f$. Choose its admissible quotient $q$. Part (i) compares $c(j)$ with $q$; part (ii), on the strictly commuting square $(1_x,r)$, compares $c(j)$ with $c(f)$ by a homotopy equivalence. Composing these diagram isomorphisms exhibits the cone triangle of $f$ as isomorphic to the triangle of the admissible sequence $x\to\widetilde y\to q$. Thus the two classes of distinguished triangles coincide. Since every $H^0$-morphism has a closed representative, this also proves the cone-existence clause of TR1. More precisely, every distinguished triangle $T=(x,y,z,f,i,d)$ admits this cone normal form with identities on $x,y$: choose an isomorphism from $T$ to an admissible-sequence triangle and then use (i) to reach a cone triangle of $f':x'\to y'$. Represent its first two isomorphisms by closed homotopy equivalences $a:x\to x'$, $b:y\to y'$. Their square commutes in $H^0$, so (ii) gives an isomorphism from the cone triangle of a closed representative of $f$ to that cone triangle of $f'$, with first two components $[a],[b]$. Composing with the inverse of the chosen isomorphism to $T$ gives identity components on $x,y$. This uses no triangulated-category axiom.

source.place: Tags 09QU (1), 09QT, and 09QN (N=2); the proof of 09QU (2) and TR1 of 09QW.

proof.text: Isomorphism invariance is built into the definition of distinguished triangles. The sequence $x\xrightarrow{1}x\to0$ is admissible with $\pi=1$, $s=0$, so its boundary is zero. This supplies the identity triangle and finishes TR1. For forward rotation, reduce to a cone triangle using step 4. Its rotation $(y,c(f),x[1],i_f,-p_f,-f[1])$ is isomorphic, by $(1,1,-1)$, to the admissible-sequence triangle $(y,c(f),x[1],i_f,p_f,f[1])$ supplied by (C). Thus forward rotation preserves distinguishedness.

source.place: Tag 09QW, TR1 and forward TR2; Tag 09QR (axiom (C) itself).

proof.text: For inverse rotation, take an admissible sequence $x\xrightarrow{a}y\xrightarrow{b}z$ with splitting $(\pi,s)$ and boundary $\delta$. Put $D=\delta[-1]:z[-1]\to x$ and choose the cone sequence $x\xrightarrow{i}c(D)\xrightarrow{p}z$, with graded splitting $(\rho,t)$. Write $\widehat D=\pi\partial s\in\mathcal A(z,x)^1$ for the degree-one version of $D$ under (B). The boundary identities give $\partial\pi=-\widehat D b$, $\partial s=a\widehat D$, $\partial t=i\widehat D$, and $\partial\rho=-\widehat D p$. Define degree-zero maps $E=i\pi+tb:y\to c(D)$ and $F=a\rho+sp:c(D)\to y$. Their differentials vanish because $\partial E=-i\widehat D b+i\widehat D b=0$ and $\partial F=-a\widehat D p+a\widehat D p=0$. The splitting identities give $FE=a\pi+sb=1_y$ and $EF=i\rho+tp=1_{c(D)}$, with the cross terms zero by $\rho t=0$, $pi=0$, $\pi s=0$, and $ba=0$; they also give $Ea=i$ and $pE=b$. Thus $(-1_{z[-1]},1_x,E)$ identifies the inverse rotation $(z[-1],x,y,-D,a,b)$ with the cone triangle $(z[-1],x,c(D),D,i,-p)$: the first square is $1_x(-D)=D(-1)$, the second is $Ea=i$, and the last is $(-1_z)b=(-p)E$. This cone triangle is distinguished by step 4. Rotation and inverse rotation are inverse on triangle diagrams, so both directions of TR2 follow using isomorphism invariance.

source.place: Tag 09QS, lemma-cone-rotate-isom (explicit inverse matrices); Tag 09QW, backward TR2. The signed inverse rotation uses -delta[-1].

proof.text: For TR3, use the identity-on-first-two-objects comparison of step 4 to put both distinguished triangles in cone form, without changing the specified first square in $H^0$. Choose closed representatives $a:x_1\to x_2$, $b:y_1\to y_2$ and degree-$-1$ $h$ with $\partial h=bf_1-f_2a$. Write the two cone splittings $(\pi_i,s_i)$ and closed inclusions/projections $(i_i,p_i)$. In shifted Hom notation define $c=i_2b\pi_1+s_2a[1]p_1+i_2hp_1$. The Leibniz rule and the boundary identities give $\partial c=-i_2bf_1p_1+i_2f_2ap_1+i_2(bf_1-f_2a)p_1=0$, while $ci_1=i_2b$ and $p_2c=a[1]p_1$. Thus $(a,b,c)$ is a morphism of the cone triangles (including their negative projections); undoing the two isomorphisms gives the required morphism of the original triangles. Steps 1 and 4-7 give every pre-triangulated axiom in [def-weil-triangulated-category].

source.place: Tag 09P7, lemma-cone, with the correctly typed last summand i_2 h p_1; Tag 09QW, TR3.

proof.text: For TR4, start with any composable pair in $H^0\mathcal A$ and choose closed representatives $f:x\to y$ and $g:y\to z$. Apply the finite admissible replacement lemma with $N=3$ to $(x,y,z;f,g)$. Its strict commuting equalities $r_2j_1=fr_1$ and $r_3j_2=gr_2$ make this pair isomorphic in $H^0$ to the pair of admissible monomorphisms $j_1:y_1\to y_2$, $j_2:y_2\to y_3$. Each $[r_i]$ is invertible by the lemma's homotopy-equivalence assertion.

Apply the admissible flag quotient lemma to $\alpha=j_1$, $\beta=j_2$. Its three admissible quotient sequences give distinguished triangles of $\alpha$, $\beta\alpha$, and $\beta$, by the definition already justified in steps 2-3. The closed maps $u:q_1\to q_2$, $v:q_2\to q_3$ satisfy the four equations $up_1=p_2\beta$, $\delta_2u=\delta_1$, $vp_2=p_3$, $\delta_3v=\alpha[1]\delta_2$ in $H^0$. These are the four octahedral squares. Its fourth admissible sequence $q_1\xrightarrow{u}q_2\xrightarrow{v}q_3$ gives a distinguished triangle with last arrow $p_1[1]\delta_3$, exactly the composite required by TR4. Hence some choice of triangles over this isomorphic replacement pair admits an octahedron.

source.place: Tag 09QX, lemma-dgc-analogue-tr4: three quotients and fourth admissible sequence; Tag 09QY.

proof.text: Apply the isomorphic-octahedron criterion to the pre-triangulated category established in step 7, using the replacement isomorphisms from step 8 and the three triangles and fourth distinguished triangle from step 9. All its hypotheses hold for every composable pair; no triangulatedness was assumed in the dg constructions. The criterion yields TR4 for every prescribed triple of distinguished triangles, not just the quotient choices. Therefore $H^0\mathcal A$ is triangulated with precisely the distinguished cone triangles identified in step 4.
